steps.narration: Now the same picture, two centuries earlier. Each tube is a state, an army, a navy, an alliance, a church or a people, and its thickness is what it measured: people, soldiers, ships, money. By seventeen seventy-five, the Thirteen Colonies had two point four million people. On the fourteenth of June, Congress voted to create a Continental Army, taking over twenty-two thousand troops outside Boston and five thousand at New York City. About two hundred and fifty thousand Americans would serve, but never more than ninety thousand at any one time.

The first proof came at Saratoga. The British general Burgoyne found his army of five thousand seven hundred and ninety-one men facing about twelve thousand colonial troops, and on the seventeenth of October seventeen seventy-seven he surrendered it. Look at where the colonists' strength came from. By some estimates, up to ninety percent of the arms they used in that campaign had come from France.

France had already been helping in secret. Its foreign minister, the Comte de Vergennes, persuaded Louis the Sixteenth to fund a front company that bought munitions for the Patriots and shipped them in neutral Dutch ships. In February seventeen seventy-eight, France signed a Treaty of Alliance with the Americans. Watch the gold tie between them. By one account, France would spend one point three billion livres supporting the Americans directly.

Now look at the sea. At the Chesapeake, the French admiral de Grasse prepared twenty-four ships of the line. The British admiral Graves sailed there with nineteen. Behind them, at Yorktown, about nineteen thousand Franco-American troops, ten thousand eight hundred of them French, faced the British army. Eight thousand soldiers and two hundred and fourteen guns were captured. The Treaty of Paris was signed on the third of September seventeen eighty-three.

The war had to be paid for. By one account it cost France one billion and sixty-six million livres, paid with new loans at high interest and no new taxes; by another, France's direct aid to the Americans alone came to one point three billion. Its debt rose to about three point three billion livres. Open the year seventeen eighty-eight. Half of the French state's revenue now went on servicing its debt. Beside the crown stands the Church, holding upwards of seven percent of France's land and taking a hundred and fifty million livres a year. By the end of the century, France had twenty-eight million people, against Britain's twelve million and Russia's thirty-five to forty million.

In seventeen eighty-nine, the Estates-General met: three hundred and two deputies for the clergy, two hundred and eighty-nine for the nobility, and six hundred and eleven for the Third Estate, which stood for about ninety-eight percent of a population of some twenty-eight million. Look at the bodies: the nation, and beside it a clergy of a hundred and fifteen to a hundred and fifty thousand.

On the fourteenth of July, the Bastille was stormed. It held only seven inmates. Then the Assembly abolished feudalism, put the Church under the control of the state, and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man. On the second of November seventeen eighty-nine, the Church's property was nationalised and used as the backing for the assignats.

On the twenty-first of January seventeen ninety-three, Louis the Sixteenth, thirty-eight years old, was guillotined on the Place de la Révolution. Watch the alliance lane: that same year, Austria, Sardinia, Naples, Prussia, Spain and Great Britain formed the First Coalition against revolutionary France. On the sixteenth of October, the queen, Marie Antoinette, was executed too.

In February seventeen ninety-three, the Convention decreed a levy of about three hundred thousand men. The Committee of Public Safety was formed in April, and in August the levée en masse drafted every man aged eighteen to twenty-five. Depending on the source, seven hundred and fifty to eight hundred thousand were conscripted. Look at the Republic's body: it is drawn by that levy of three hundred thousand.

From June seventeen ninety-three, the Terror issued sixteen thousand five hundred and ninety-four official death sentences, two thousand six hundred and thirty-nine of them in Paris, and thirteen hundred and sixty-six in the seven weeks after the Law of twenty-two Prairial. The dark red lobe beneath the Republic is that toll. Then Robespierre and twenty-one of his followers were themselves sentenced to death under the same law, without even a cursory hearing. Robespierre was executed on the twenty-eighth of July seventeen ninety-four, the date with which the Terror is often said to end.

On the ninth of November seventeen ninety-nine, the bloodless coup of eighteen Brumaire overthrew the Directory and replaced it with the Consulate, Bonaparte's regime. On the seventh of February eighteen hundred, a plebiscite approved its constitution. Watch the French lane: the Republic has become the Consulate.

Under the Concordat of eighteen-oh-one, the Pope recognised Bonaparte's regime, and the regime recognised Catholicism as the religion of the great majority of the French. In eighteen-oh-four the Senate vested the government in an emperor, and a plebiscite confirmed the hereditary empire: three and a half million votes yes, a count inflated by three to five hundred thousand. On the second of December, at Notre-Dame, with Pope Pius the Seventh present, Napoleon crowned himself. The ceremony left out the words by which a monarch received his crown from the Church. Britain, Russia, Sweden and the Ottoman Empire refused to recognise the title.

Britain declared war on France in May eighteen-oh-three and repeatedly financed France's enemies on the Continent. In April eighteen-oh-five it formed a Third Coalition with Austria and Russia. Now the sea. After seventeen ninety-three, Britain raised its sailors from fifteen thousand to a hundred and thirty-three thousand. At Trafalgar, Nelson's twenty-seven ships of the line met thirty-three French and Spanish. Eighteen of the enemy were captured or destroyed. Britain lost none.

At Austerlitz, Napoleon had some seventy-two thousand men and a hundred and fifty-seven guns, against about eighty-five thousand Allied soldiers, seventy percent of them Russian, with three hundred and eighteen guns. Allied casualties stood at about thirty-six thousand, some thirty-eight percent of their effective force, by a count that puts their army at eighty-nine thousand. In eighteen-oh-six the Prussian army awaiting Napoleon's advance numbered about a hundred and thirty thousand Prussians and twenty thousand Saxons. On the fourteenth of October, at Jena and Auerstedt, the Grande Armée decisively defeated it.

Europe was out of balance. By the Berlin Decree of the twenty-first of November eighteen-oh-six, Napoleon barred Britain's trade from the Continent. The loss of Britain as a trading partner hit France and its allies too. In eighteen-oh-eight his Army of Spain, two hundred and seventy-eight thousand six hundred and seventy men, faced eighty thousand raw Spanish troops. Then Russia. In eighteen-twelve Napoleon deployed six hundred thousand soldiers against it, only half of them French, not counting the Austrian and Prussian contingents. Russia's army peaked at seven hundred and twelve thousand, or at nine hundred and four thousand by another count. Of an original force of six hundred and fifteen thousand, by another count, only a hundred and ten thousand came back. The dark red lobe beneath the Grande Armée is what it lost: more than five hundred thousand men.

From seventeen ninety-three to eighteen fourteen, Britain gave its allies more than forty-six million pounds in subsidies, which paid for a large share of the Austrian and Russian soldiers, about four hundred and fifty thousand at their peak in eighteen-thirteen. At Leipzig, about five hundred and sixty thousand soldiers fought by one count, and there were a hundred and thirty-three thousand casualties. The Coalition armies decisively defeated the Grande Armée. In eighteen-fifteen, about two hundred and fifty thousand Frenchmen faced about eight hundred and fifty thousand allied soldiers. At Waterloo, Napoleon's army of about seventy-four thousand five hundred met Wellington, and fifty thousand arriving Prussians struck its flank. Four days later, Napoleon abdicated.

From September eighteen-fourteen to June eighteen-fifteen, the Congress of Vienna, chaired by Metternich, set out not simply to restore the old borders, but to resize the main powers so that they would balance each other and remain at peace. The five Great Powers, Austria, Britain, Russia, Prussia, and France itself, dealt behind closed doors. Britain's national debt had reached six hundred and seventy-nine million pounds. The Concert of Europe, a doctrine of the balance of power, guided European foreign policy until nineteen fourteen.
